title: Aurora Health Systems x Redwood — technical deep dive: overload behavior + SLAs
summary: Aurora asked detailed questions about Redwood’s new hosted overload protections: what errors look like (429 vs 503), whether Retry-After is always present, how to avoid retry storms, and how noisy-neighbor isolation works across tenants and tiers. Redwood described circuit breaker layering (gateway admission + routing + runtime backpressure), tenant/tier-aware policies, stable overload error codes with correlation IDs, and optional graceful degradation (fallback model/region, feature reduction like max_tokens caps / streaming concurrency). Aurora emphasized healthcare reliability expectations and asked how overload-induced failures map to SLAs/SLO reporting. Redwood committed to share the overload error taxonomy doc + sample responses, confirm Retry-After behavior across routes, and propose a pilot plan and SLA language for Hosted vs Dedicated.
topics:
1) Overload error taxonomy and stable semantics (HTTP status + error codes)
2) Retry-After contract and client backoff guidance
3) Circuit breakers vs load shedding: where they happen (gateway/routing/runtime)
4) Noisy-neighbor isolation (per-tenant limits, tier-aware defaults)
5) Graceful degradation modes (fallback routing, reduced features)
6) SLO/SLAs and how overload errors are reported
7) Pilot expectations + next steps
questions:
Aurora: When you’re overloaded, do we see 429 or 503, and is it consistent across endpoints?
Aurora: Is Retry-After guaranteed on overload responses? Seconds vs HTTP-date? Any edge cases?
Aurora: How do you prevent client retries from amplifying an incident (retry storm)?
Aurora: Can we configure fallback models/regions, and how do you prevent loops?
Aurora: How do you ensure a self-serve customer can’t take out an enterprise tenant (noisy neighbor)?
Aurora: In your SLA/SLO reporting, do overload-induced rejections count as downtime or not?
Aurora: If we move to Dedicated, do these behaviors change (and can we still shed load gracefully)?
action_items: Nikhil Sharma (Redwood) — Send Aurora the overload error taxonomy + example payloads (codes, 429/503 mapping, correlation ID) — Due 2025-12-04
Ibrahim Khan (Redwood) — Confirm Retry-After header behavior across chat/embeddings/rerank routes and share guidance snippet — Due 2025-12-05
Rafael Mendes (Redwood) — Share SLO/SLA note on how overload errors are classified and how it impacts reporting — Due 2025-12-06
Mina Haddad (Redwood) — Provide a short write-up on fallback routing constraints (loop prevention, bounded retries, compatibility) — Due 2025-12-06
Priya Rao (Aurora) — Provide current client retry/backoff implementation + which SDKs they use, for Redwood to review — Due 2025-12-09
next_steps: Redwood to share a one-pager with canonical overload response examples and recommended client retry policy (exponential backoff + jitter + honoring Retry-After).
Schedule a 60-min follow-up to review pilot design (traffic shape, success criteria, canary plan) and discuss Hosted vs Dedicated SLA language.
Aurora to send their peak/burst profile (concurrency, prompt sizes, streaming usage) so Redwood can propose initial per-tenant limits and degradation toggles.
If Aurora wants Dedicated, Redwood to loop in Dedicated PM for capacity reservation and region requirements.
transcript_text:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Date: 2025-12-02
Time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 53 min
Call type: Technical deep dive
Title: Aurora Health Systems x Redwood — technical deep dive: overload behavior + SLAs

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Nikhil Sharma, Rafael Mendes, Mina Haddad, Ibrahim Khan, Peter Holtz
Aurora Health Systems: Priya Rao, Daniel Kim, Erin Walsh, Miguel Santos

---

[00:00] Nikhil Sharma: Cool. Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. The goal today is basically to go deep on our overload behavior, circuit breakers, load shedding, and what that means for SLAs and client handling.

[00:14] Priya Rao: Yep. This is the thing that bit us with a previous provider. We got… like, ambiguous timeouts. Not even 5xx, just hanging streams.

[00:24] Rafael Mendes: Yeah, that’s exactly what we’re trying to avoid. Prefer explicit, early rejection with stable semantics versus letting the system thrash.

[00:33] Daniel Kim: And we’re healthcare, so… it’s not “nice to have”. If we can’t reason about it, we can’t ship it.

[00:42] Nikhil Sharma: Totally. Maybe just quick context check—are you thinking Hosted first, or Dedicated out of the gate?

[00:50] Priya Rao: We’re evaluating both. Hosted for speed, Dedicated if we can’t get the predictability we need.

[00:58] Miguel Santos: Also region constraints. At minimum US. Maybe multi-region later.

[01:04] Nikhil Sharma: Makes sense. Mina, Rafael, Ibrahim are here because this touches routing, SRE, and SDK behavior.

[01:12] Erin Walsh: Great. I’ll be the annoying SRE person. I’m going to ask about error budgets and whether you just… reclassify everything as “not our fault”.

[01:21] (crosstalk)

[01:22] Rafael Mendes: Please do.

[01:24] Nikhil Sharma: Let’s start with the customer-facing behavior. When we’re overloaded, you’ll get an explicit JSON error response with a stable error code, plus a request ID / correlation ID.

[01:36] Priya Rao: And the HTTP status—this is our first question. Is it 429 or 503? We’ve seen vendors mix them.

[01:45] Peter Holtz: It’s intentionally mapped. 429 is for tenant-scoped rate / quota / concurrency type rejections. 503 is for platform overload where the system is protecting itself or a downstream is unhealthy.

[01:58] Priya Rao: Okay, but like, what if it’s your platform overload but only in one region? Still 503?

[02:04] Mina Haddad: Still 503, but the payload will include an overload code that indicates “regional_capacity” vs “dependency_brownout” vs “runtime_saturation”. Not all of those are exposed today in every product, but the goal is stable codes.

[02:20] Ibrahim Khan: And importantly, the body is consistent across endpoints. Chat completions, text, embeddings—same top-level fields so clients can implement one handler.

[02:31] Erin Walsh: What are the fields? Like do you have a “retryable” boolean or…?

[02:35] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah, typically: an error.type, error.code, error.message, request_id, and a retry_after_seconds hint. Plus we set Retry-After header.

[02:47] Daniel Kim: You said “set Retry-After header”. Is it guaranteed?

[02:53] Ibrahim Khan: Contractually—our intent is yes for overload-induced rejections. There are a couple edge cases we’re tightening, like legacy routes. But for the new overload framework it’s consistent. We prefer seconds value.

[03:10] Priya Rao: Seconds as in “Retry-After: 2” not date.

[03:13] Ibrahim Khan: Correct.

[03:15] Erin Walsh: What about streaming? That’s where we saw timeouts. Like the connection is open, tokens start, then it stalls, then we don’t know if we should retry.

[03:26] Rafael Mendes: Streaming is tricky because you can be mid-flight. Our approach is twofold: (1) admission control before we start work, based on queue depth and concurrency signals, so we don’t accept something we can’t serve; and (2) runtime backpressure so if the GPU scheduler is saturated we stop admitting new work rather than letting tail latency explode.

[03:46] Mina Haddad: And at routing, if a model/region is in breaker-open state, we can optionally route to a fallback region or compatible model variant—if you configure it.

[03:58] Priya Rao: I’m going to dig into that. “Compatible model variant” means what? Like same family, same context window?

[04:05] Mina Haddad: Exactly. There’s a compatibility matrix. We won’t just randomly swap to something that breaks your tool calling. You can define allowed fallbacks, and we cap attempts to avoid loops.

[04:18] Erin Walsh: What does loop prevention look like? Because again, we’ve seen “failover ping pong”.

[04:23] Mina Haddad: We attach a small routing context—basically a bounded retry budget. If primary is overloaded, we try fallback once (or a configured number), and if fallback also indicates overload we stop and return the overload error rather than bouncing.

[04:40] Priya Rao: Good. Now, Retry-After. How do you decide the number? That’s usually hand-wavy.

[04:47] Rafael Mendes: It’s derived from the overload signal and policy. For example, if it’s a hard breaker-open due to sustained saturation, it might be a longer retry window, like 5–15 seconds. If it’s a transient queue spike, it can be shorter.

[05:03] Erin Walsh: Do you worry about everyone retrying at exactly 5 seconds and creating a thundering herd?

[05:09] Rafael Mendes: Yes. That’s why we recommend jitter on the client. Retry-After is a floor, not “retry exactly then”. We’ll provide guidance: exponential backoff with jitter, max attempts, and importantly: do not retry non-idempotent operations blindly.

[05:25] Priya Rao: For chat completions, it’s kind of idempotent if we supply the same prompt, but tool calling side effects… eh.

[05:33] Nikhil Sharma: Right. We generally tell customers to use idempotency keys when their workflow has side effects. The SDKs will have examples. We’re not redesigning the API, but we’re documenting best practice.

[05:48] Daniel Kim: We’ll need that in writing. Our risk team needs to see an explicit contract.

[05:55] Nikhil Sharma: Yep.

[05:57] Erin Walsh: Okay. Noisy neighbor. How do you prevent some random tenant from ruining our p99?

[06:05] Peter Holtz: There are multiple layers. At the gateway: per-tenant concurrency caps and token buckets. At routing: tier-aware admission and per-model/per-route limits. At runtime: queue isolation and saturation signals exported per pool so one tenant can’t starve the entire GPU fleet.

[06:24] Erin Walsh: Is that hard isolation or best-effort?

[06:27] Rafael Mendes: In Hosted it’s policy + scheduling isolation, so it’s not “you get your own GPUs” like Dedicated. But it’s explicitly designed to stop cascades. Dedicated is hard isolation by separate capacity pools.

[06:43] Priya Rao: So if we’re Hosted enterprise tier, we get different defaults?

[06:48] Nikhil Sharma: Yes. Tier-aware policies. Enterprise Hosted has more conservative protections against noisy neighbors and a different priority in admission when capacity is constrained.

[06:59] Miguel Santos: “Priority” makes me nervous. Does that mean other customers get dropped first?

[07:04] Nikhil Sharma: It means we preserve tenant isolation and our contractual SLAs. But it’s not like we starve everyone. It’s more: your rate and concurrency commitments are protected.

[07:15] Erin Walsh: I’ll translate: you have a queue and you decide who you admit. Fine.

[07:20] Mina Haddad: And on the routing side, we can route your traffic away from a hot region earlier because we detect capacity signals before it becomes a timeouts situation.

[07:33] Priya Rao: I want to talk about graceful degradation. What do you actually do besides “return 503”?

[07:40] Rafael Mendes: Three buckets. One is early rejection with clear error codes. Two is fallback routing if configured. Three is feature reduction under duress: for example capping max_tokens, limiting streaming concurrency, or disabling non-essential tool calling complexity—behind policy flags.

[08:00] Priya Rao: Wait. Disabling tool calling—how would we know?

[08:03] Ibrahim Khan: We would not silently change semantics. If a degradation mode is enabled, the response includes a flag/field indicating degraded mode and what constraint was applied (like max_tokens capped). For tool calling, we’d only do it if you explicitly opt-in and we’d return an explicit error if the request requires tools but tools are disabled.

[08:25] Daniel Kim: Good. Silent behavior changes are a no-go.

[08:28] Erin Walsh: How about queued admission? Like 202 and wait?

[08:33] Rafael Mendes: Not in the first version for Hosted API. We’re mostly using reject early rather than queue unbounded. Internal queueing exists but we don’t expose a “job handle” pattern yet.

[08:48] Priya Rao: Fine.

[08:50] Erin Walsh: SLAs. Here’s my spicy question. When you shed load and return 503, do you count that as downtime?

[08:58] Rafael Mendes: We count it as an error event; we don’t pretend it didn’t happen. But we classify overload-induced rejections separately from internal 5xx due to bugs. The reason is we want reporting that’s actionable—are we failing because of overload vs code.

[09:18] Erin Walsh: But does it burn the availability SLO?

[09:21] Rafael Mendes: Generally yes, it impacts success rate as observed by clients. The nuance is around “overload exceptions”—some providers carve out “customer-caused traffic spikes”. We don’t blanket exclude it. For enterprise contracts we can align on definitions.

[09:40] Daniel Kim: I’m going to need that nuance. Our contracts people will ask, “If you reject us, you owe credits, right?”

[09:47] Nikhil Sharma: Understood. For Dedicated it’s cleaner: you have reserved capacity, so overload should be mostly attributable to misconfiguration or unexpected usage patterns; but we still provide circuit breakers to protect the runtime.

[10:03] Priya Rao: And for Hosted?

[10:05] Nikhil Sharma: For Hosted enterprise, we can talk about an SLA that includes explicit overload behavior—like “we will return explicit overload errors with Retry-After” rather than timeouts—and we can talk about credits depending on the plan.

[10:20] Erin Walsh: I actually like “explicit overload errors instead of timeouts” as a commitment.

[10:25] Miguel Santos: What about dependency brownouts? Like your auth service or something. Same mechanism?

[10:32] Peter Holtz: Yeah. If downstream dependencies are unhealthy, the breaker can open and you’ll see 503 with a different error code (dependency_unavailable) and a Retry-After.

[10:45] Priya Rao: Is it ever 504?

[10:47] Ibrahim Khan: We try not to. Timeouts are the worst UX. The goal is to proactively return errors rather than letting a request hit a gateway timeout.

[10:58] Erin Walsh: Okay but in reality, there’s always some tail. Do you have any numbers? Like do you have p99 improvements with shedding?

[11:07] Rafael Mendes: We do internal load tests: with shedding enabled, p99 under bursts stays bounded and 5xx/timeouts drop, but you’ll see an increase in explicit 429/503 during the burst. That’s the trade.

[11:22] Priya Rao: That’s fine if it’s predictable.

[11:26] Nikhil Sharma: Let’s talk about semantics again. Example payload might look like:

[11:32] Speaker 2 (transcription): error dot code equals “overloaded”, message “Service temporarily overloaded”, request_id “...” retry_after_seconds “...”

[11:41] Ibrahim Khan: Close. And we include a docs URL sometimes.

[11:45] Priya Rao: Correlation IDs—are they consistent across retries?

[11:50] Ibrahim Khan: Request ID is per attempt. If you supply an idempotency key, we can link them in logs; and we also emit a trace/correlation header you can send back to support.

[12:04] Daniel Kim: Are those IDs PHI-safe? Like are you encoding anything.

[12:08] Ibrahim Khan: No, it’s random. No payload content.

[12:12] Daniel Kim: Good.

[12:14] Erin Walsh: Noisy neighbor again—do you do per-route? Because embeddings bursts are different from chat.

[12:21] Peter Holtz: Yes, per route/model. You can have different limits for /chat vs /embeddings. And policy can be tenant-specific.

[12:33] Priya Rao: Can we see the policy schema?

[12:35] Nikhil Sharma: We can share a draft and the parts that are stable.

[12:39] Mina Haddad: One caution: we keep it safe by preventing unsafe configs. Like you can’t set “infinite fallback loops”.

[12:47] Erin Walsh: Love that.

[12:50] (pause)

[12:52] Priya Rao: Okay. Scenario: We send a burst because we had a notification event, and we exceed concurrency. We get 429 with Retry-After. If we respect it, are we guaranteed to be accepted after?

[13:07] Rafael Mendes: Not a guarantee, because the system could still be under load, but it’s the best signal. We want it to be monotonic-ish: if you back off, your probability of success goes up.

[13:20] Erin Walsh: That’s an honest answer.

[13:22] Miguel Santos: Another scenario: multi-region failover. If us-east is hot, do you automatically move us to us-west?

[13:30] Mina Haddad: Not automatically without config, because it can have latency/data residency implications. But you can enable regional fallback. We’d also prevent flip-flopping.

[13:42] Daniel Kim: Data residency—if we enable fallback, how do we guarantee it stays in US?

[13:48] Mina Haddad: Routing policies include region allow-lists. You can pin to US regions only.

[13:56] Daniel Kim: Good.

[13:58] Erin Walsh: What about “feature reduction” for max_tokens. If you cap it, do you return a partial answer? Or you reject?

[14:05] Rafael Mendes: We wouldn’t truncate silently. If we cap, it’s applied at admission—so we’d either adjust the request (if you opted into that) and indicate it, or we return an explicit error saying requested max_tokens exceeds current limit.

[14:22] Priya Rao: We would prefer an explicit error rather than changing it.

[14:25] Nikhil Sharma: That’s the default.

[14:28] Erin Walsh: Retry guidance. Do you have something concrete, like “max 3 retries, exponential backoff, jitter, respect Retry-After”?

[14:36] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. For 429/503 overload errors: start with Retry-After if present, otherwise backoff 250ms -> 500ms -> 1s with jitter; cap at like 10s; and max attempts depends on your end-user timeout budget. Also: never do immediate retries in a loop.

[14:56] Priya Rao: We’ve seen SDKs do the opposite.

[14:58] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah, we’re fixing that. Our SDKs will surface typed errors so you can handle them intentionally.

[15:05] Erin Walsh: Are you doing anything server-side to dampen retries?

[15:09] Rafael Mendes: Yes. Breakers open based on sustained saturation. That forces explicit responses. It’s better than letting each request consume resources and then timeout.

[15:21] Priya Rao: How do you detect “saturation”? GPU metrics are noisy.

[15:26] Rafael Mendes: Multiple signals: scheduler queue depth, token-per-second saturation, memory pressure proxies, plus dependency health. We combine them with guardrails to reduce false positives.

[15:41] Erin Walsh: Do you page on breaker-open?

[15:44] Rafael Mendes: For canary yes, and in GA we page based on sustained shed rate and impact. But we also announce state transitions in our incident channels.

[15:54] Daniel Kim: Are customers notified? Like status page.

[15:58] Nikhil Sharma: For major events, yes. For minor transient shedding, usually not; but you’ll see it in your metrics and responses.

[16:07] Priya Rao: Do we get metrics? Like how many requests were shed.

[16:11] Peter Holtz: In the console you can see error breakdowns by code, plus shed rate. For enterprise we can also provide dashboards.

[16:22] Erin Walsh: Okay. I’m going to ask about dedicated again. If we buy Dedicated, do we still get 503 overload?

[16:29] Nikhil Sharma: Potentially, if you exceed your reserved throughput or you misconfigure limits. But it’s different: you control the capacity pool, so we can tune it more directly. And you’d generally see 429 if it’s you exceeding your own configured caps.

[16:47] Miguel Santos: So Dedicated is more predictable.

[16:50] Nikhil Sharma: Yes.

[16:52] (crosstalk)

[16:53] Priya Rao: Alright. Can we talk through an SLA example? Like what you’d say to our procurement.

[16:59] Nikhil Sharma: We can’t finalize contract language on this call, but we can share typical language: uptime, latency targets on Dedicated, and for Hosted enterprise: error rate targets and explicit overload behavior.

[17:12] Daniel Kim: We’ll need it.

[17:14] Erin Walsh: And we’ll want to know if overload errors count towards the SLO.

[17:19] Rafael Mendes: We’ll send a written note on our classification, and we can align on the contract interpretation.

[17:26] Priya Rao: Okay. Next: we do our own client-side circuit breaker. If we see 503 we open our breaker. But if it’s 429 we treat it differently. That mapping is key.

[17:36] Ibrahim Khan: That’s exactly why we’re pushing stable codes. We can also include a “retryable” hint and “category: overload” so you don’t have to parse message strings.

[17:49] Priya Rao: Great.

[17:51] Miguel Santos: One more technical question—when you fallback to a different model, does that affect cost? Like pricing differences.

[17:58] Nikhil Sharma: It can, depending on the model. Typically fallback is within a similar pricing tier, but we don’t want surprises; you can constrain allowed fallbacks and we’ll document expected behavior.

[18:12] Priya Rao: We’d probably only fallback region, not model, at least initially.

[18:17] Mina Haddad: That’s a common pattern.

[18:20] Erin Walsh: Okay I’m looking at my list. “Retry-After missing sometimes.” We saw this with another provider. You said you’re tightening edge cases. Are there routes where it’s not there today?

[18:31] Ibrahim Khan: There were some inconsistencies historically—mainly older chat endpoints. The direction is: overload responses include Retry-After. I’ll confirm exact coverage and send it.

[18:43] Daniel Kim: Thank you.

[18:45] Priya Rao: And the semantics of Retry-After: If you say 10 seconds, you promise capacity?

[18:50] Rafael Mendes: Not a promise. It’s guidance to reduce harm. We can’t guarantee, but we can make it accurate enough to be useful.

[19:00] Erin Walsh: That’s fine.

[19:02] (pause)

[19:04] Nikhil Sharma: Do you want to cover how this ties into your internal SLOs? Like what do you need to show to leadership.

[19:10] Priya Rao: We need to show: predictable behavior, no silent degradation, documented retry contract, and that you won’t let other tenants starve us.

[19:20] Daniel Kim: And security basics: audit logs, encryption, data retention.

[19:25] Nikhil Sharma: We can follow up on security separately, but yes—SOC 2, audit logs, KMS integrations exist in certain tiers. For today, we’ll keep on overload.

[19:36] Erin Walsh: I want an example of a full response. Like headers and body.

[19:41] Ibrahim Khan: We’ll send examples for 429 and 503 with Retry-After and request IDs.

[19:47] Priya Rao: Great.

[19:49] (transcript jumps slightly)

[20:02] Mina Haddad: Just to be explicit: we avoid feedback loops. If runtime is saturated, it exports a signal; gateway uses it for admission; routing uses it for fallback; but we don’t want the system oscillating.

[20:16] Erin Walsh: How do you avoid oscillation?

[20:18] Mina Haddad: Hysteresis and cool-downs. Breakers don’t flap open/closed every second. Also we base it on short windows and sustained conditions.

[20:30] Rafael Mendes: And we watch false positives in canary. If we shed too aggressively, we tune.

[20:37] Priya Rao: Canary by region?

[20:39] Rafael Mendes: Yes. Start one region, subset of tenants, then expand.

[20:45] Daniel Kim: That’s good.

[20:47] Erin Walsh: Okay. We should talk about “what should our client do”. If we get 503 with overload code, we back off and maybe failover to another region on our side.

[20:58] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. And if you enable our regional fallback, you might not need to do it yourself. But you can.

[21:07] Priya Rao: Our preference is we control it, at least at first.

[21:10] Mina Haddad: Understood.

[21:12] Nikhil Sharma: We’re at about the halfway mark. Anything else on the semantics?

[21:17] Erin Walsh: One thing: do you ever return 200 with an error in the stream? Like SSE event “error”.

[21:24] Ibrahim Khan: If a stream fails mid-flight, it can end with an error event. But the overload framework tries to prevent accepting something we can’t finish. Mid-stream failures are usually network or unexpected dependency failures.

[21:40] Erin Walsh: Okay.

[21:41] Priya Rao: And you include correlation IDs there too?

[21:44] Ibrahim Khan: Yes.

[21:46] Daniel Kim: Okay.

[21:48] (brief silence)

[22:02] Nikhil Sharma: Let’s do next steps. We’ll send a packet: error taxonomy, sample payloads, Retry-After guidance, and a note on how we treat overload errors in SLO reporting. Then we schedule a follow-up to define a pilot.

[22:18] Priya Rao: Can we also get something about Dedicated vs Hosted differences? Like a quick table.

[22:23] Nikhil Sharma: Yes.

[22:25] Miguel Santos: Pilot-wise, we can send you our traffic profile. It’s bursty, weekdays only, lots of streaming.

[22:32] Rafael Mendes: Perfect. That helps tune initial thresholds.

[22:36] Erin Walsh: And we’ll send you our current retry strategy. It’s probably too aggressive.

[22:41] Ibrahim Khan: Great.

[22:43] Daniel Kim: One more: status page messaging. If you’re shedding, do you say “degraded”? We had issues with vendor status pages being… optimistic.

[22:52] Nikhil Sharma: For major sustained shedding we’d communicate degradation. For small transient it might not hit status page. We can share what we typically say.

[23:04] Priya Rao: Okay.

[23:06] (transcription drift; speakers occasionally mislabeled)

[23:18] Speaker 1: cool cool.

[23:20] Priya Rao: Alright, I think that covers it. Thanks.

[23:24] Nikhil Sharma: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up by end of week with those docs and schedule.
